summary: Lake Michigan harbour light at Michigan City, Indiana: 1858 tower, kept by Harriet Colfax 1861 to 1904; light moved to the east pier in 1904; now a museum.

lens.note: L. Sautter & Cie fifth-order lens of the 1858 tower; LighthouseFriends says the lens used in both the old light and the pierhead light is on display

structures.note: USLHS gives a tower height of 34 ft; Wikipedia (lead only) gives 40 ft and is not used
LighthouseFriends: conical brick tower of 39 ft; NRHP nomination: 'wooden conical tower'

access.note: Old Lighthouse Museum in Washington Park; open Wednesday to Sunday, 1-4 pm, April to 31 October 2026 (Michigan City Historical Society).

visit.note: Spiral staircase to the lantern room installed 2003 (LighthouseFriends)

facts.agency: City of Michigan City (owner); Michigan City Historical Society (lessee and operator)

events.note: First tower built (NRHP nomination)
Ready in December 1837; not exhibited until summer 1838 (LighthouseFriends). The record's 1835 is the year of the land grant.
Sixth-order Fresnel lens
Present tower and dwelling built to replace the 1837 tower
Fifth-order L. Sautter & Cie Fresnel lens, fixed white, focal plane 52 ft
Pierhead tower and elevated walk built on the east pier; moved to the west pier in 1875 (LighthouseFriends)
December 1885 storm damaged the elevated walk and pier; light stopped until repairs
Pierhead beacon swept away in a gale on 14 October 1886 (not the 1858 light)
Lighthouse Board: some 6,000 bricks for an oil house; $5,500 appropriated for a fog signal at this station
Fixed white light moved to the outer end of the east pier on 20 October 1904
Light discontinued at the 1858 tower on 20 October 1904
Cylindrical tower on the west pier washed away
Breakwater light destroyed during a storm in February 1909; buoy lantern on a concrete shaft from 1911
Storm of 8-10 November 1913 destroyed 200 ft of the elevated walk
Keeper Thomas J. Armstrong recognized for rescuing two men from drowning
Armstrong's rescue of a boy who had fallen from the pier noted in Lighthouse Service records
Storm of 18-19 December 1929 carried away the outer 312 ft of the east pier walkway
The 1858 house stopped serving as keepers' quarters
Declared surplus after rental and use by the Coast Guard Auxiliary
General Services Administration sold the lighthouse to Michigan City for $18,500
Twenty-year lease to the Michigan City Historical Society
Opened 9 June 1973 after eight years of restoration; new tower and lantern room
Listed 5 November 1974 (NRHP 74000023)
Spiral staircase installed by the Hoosier Lighthousing Club
Replica lantern room of the 1970s replaced with a new one built locally

corrections.why: 1835 is the year of the land grant (NRHP 1990 additional documentation: 'June 23, 1835'). LighthouseFriends says the light was ready in December 1837 and not exhibited until summer 1838; the NRHP nomination says the first lighthouse was built in 1837. Reviewer should decide between 1837 (built) and 1838 (first exhibited) for this field.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 1835 is the land-grant year. The NRHP says the first lighthouse was built in 1837; LighthouseFriends says it was ready in December 1837 and first exhibited in summer 1838. The story says so and gives 1838 as the first lighting.

notes_for_editor: Sources disagree on the first tower's material (LighthouseFriends: conical brick, 39 ft; NRHP nomination OCR: 'wooden conical tower') and on first lighting (1837 built per NRHP; summer 1838 per LighthouseFriends). Both stated in the story; not resolved. The NRHP text is OCR of a 1974 typescript with errors (for example 'Coifax' for Colfax, and garbled lines around the tower description); quotes are copied as OCR gives them, and the nomination's cached copy was used for checking. The roster for 'Michigan City (Old)' was matched by slug (--place michigan-city-old), not by name: a name search ranked the East Pierhead first. The USLHS place record gives coordinates 41.0731, -86.9058, which are about 72 km south of the light (a USLHS position error); the station record's OSM coordinates (41.722469, -86.906014) are used. After 1904 the keepers ran the pierhead lights and lived in the 1858 house; the USLHS files their stints under the East Pierhead record (us-in-michigan-city-east), so the post-1904 rows come from LighthouseFriends and carry no person slug. The 1904-40 names are LighthouseFriends' list, not checked against the NARA registers. Ann C. Hartwell lived in the house and is named in the story, but no source gives her a keeper's appointment, so she is not in the roster. The Indiana State Library blog says the 1904 lighthouse 'was owned by the Lifesaving Service' and that Harriet C. Towner was Colfax's successor; both are contradicted by the NRHP (land under the Light-House Establishment) and the roster, and are not used. Lens order: the Wikipedia lead says fourth order; LighthouseFriends, the NRHP and the USLHS say fifth; fifth is used. The Chicago Daily Tribune interview of 2 October 1904 was not read directly; it is quoted as LighthouseFriends and the Indiana State Library quote it. The 1900 Lighthouse Board entry is cited by scan page 167; the printed page number was not read. The 1858 tower's material is given as 'wooden' by LighthouseFriends and the NRHP text; the 1858 dwelling is 'Joliet stone' and 'Milwaukee brick' in LighthouseFriends. The Michigan City Historical Society hours are current as of 2026-10-27; Wikipedia's older hours are not used. The Palladium OCR has garbled the companion's name ('Ann art-Avell'); the story does not quote the name from the OCR. Added in the fact-check of 2026-10-27: (a) Palladium OCR garbles the companion's surname ('Ann art-Avell'); the story names her as Ann, Colfax's companion, and identifies her as Hartwell from the context; the image was not readable through the tools here. (b) Hartwell's death date: Indiana State Library 22 January 1905, NPS 27 January 1905; both are in the story. (c) Colfax's death date: LighthouseFriends and ISL 16 April 1905, NPS text 17 April (its quick facts say 16 April); both are in the story. (d) West pier move: LighthouseFriends 1875, NPS biography 1874; both are in the story. (e) Retirement: LighthouseFriends quotes her letter of resignation and the Palladium says she 'recently resigned'; the NPS biography says she was 'forced into retirement with the decision to modernize and electrify'; both are in the story. (f) The NPS passage 'It is fearful to hear...' sits in its account of an 1881 newspaper interview (Courier-Journal, 11 Aug 1881, in its bibliography), not undated and unsourced; the story now says so. (g) Lighthouse Board 1900: the Michigan City entry (No. 44x, Ninth District, scan 167) reads 'Some 6,000 bricks for the construction of an oil house were provided' and the sundry civil act of June 6, 1900 $5,500 for a fog signal. Note that the Board's text for entry 420 (Manistee) has a similar 'Some 6,000 bricks' line; the Michigan City entry is the one cited. The printed page number was not read. (h) The 1990 NRHP additional documentation counts the flagpole and the other displays as temporary, so the story no longer says the grounds 'hold' it. (i) The NRHP says the 1904 remodel converted the house into 'two three-story apartments' and that the fifth-order lens was moved to the end of the east pier in 1904; the story uses the LighthouseFriends lens account (used in both lights, on display) and does not repeat the NRHP lens line. (j) The Chicago Tribune interview (2 October 1904) is quoted as LighthouseFriends and the Indiana State Library print it; the Tribune page was not read.
